messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 56
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Musician
- Trauma Type: Sexual assault
- Pcl5: 71

James is fifty-six years old, with the kind of hands that have known a fretboard for four decades. He sits in the chair across from me, a leather jacket worn soft at the elbows, his wedding ring catching the light as he fidgets with the zipper pull. He tells me he hasn’t played a note in six months. Not one. The guitars are still in their cases, lined up in the corner of the rehearsal space like headstones.

The story comes out in pieces, over three sessions. It starts in the green room of a club in a city he doesn’t name. A promoter he’d worked with for years, a man he trusted, offered him a drink after the show. James remembers the taste being off, metallic. He remembers the room tilting, the carpet against his cheek, the weight. He remembers a voice saying, *You’ll be fine, just rest.* He woke up in his hotel room at dawn, sore, disoriented, a button missing from his shirt. He didn’t call the police. He didn’t tell his wife, Marie. He told himself he’d had too much to drink, that he’d imagined the rest. For three years, he believed that.

Now, he can’t un-believe it. The memory arrived six months ago, unbidden, while he was tuning his Les Paul in the living room. The smell of the green room—stale beer, carpet cleaner, sweat—flooded his sinuses. His hands went numb. He dropped the tuning peg and sat on the floor, shaking, while Marie called his name from the kitchen. He didn’t answer. He couldn’t. He was back on that carpet.

Since then, James has been living inside a constant low-grade alarm. He can’t be in a room without an exit behind him. He scans every crowd at the grocery store, at the gas station, looking for the promoter’s face, even though the man lives three states away. He jumps when a car backfires. He has stopped touring. He has stopped leaving the house after dark. At night, he lies awake next to Marie, his jaw clenched so tight his teeth ache, listening for footsteps in the hall. He has nightmares that he can’t fully recall, only the feeling of suffocation and a metallic taste in his mouth.

The worst part, he says, is the silence. He used to write songs to process everything—heartbreak, joy, the road. Now, when he picks up a guitar, his mind goes blank. The music is gone. In its place is a hot, wordless shame. He feels dirty, even after showering. He avoids looking at himself in the mirror. He hasn’t touched Marie intimately in months, and when she tried to hold his hand last week, he flinched. He saw the hurt in her eyes. He couldn’t explain that his skin felt like it belonged to someone else.

He tells me he feels like a ghost in his own life. He watches himself go through the motions—coffee, the newspaper, a walk around the block—but he’s not really there. He’s back in that room, or he’s bracing for it to happen again. He’s stopped answering calls from bandmates. He let his agent go. He says, with a hollow laugh, that he’s become a musician who can’t stand the sound of his own instrument.

When I ask him what he wants, he looks at the floor for a long time. Finally, he says, *I want to not be afraid of my own hands.* He holds them out, palms up, as if they are strangers.
